tips.title: Baby hem for sheers and lightweights
tips.steps:
Mark the finished hem length.
Stitch 3 mm (1/8") below the mark with a short stitch, about 1.5 mm.
Fold the raw edge to the wrong side along that stitching and edgestitch through both layers, right on the fold.
Trim the excess close to the stitching with sharp appliqué scissors, supporting the fold on your hand. Trim only when you're ready to carry on, as the fabric can pull out of the stitches.
Fold the stitched edge up once more to enclose the raw edge.
Stitch over the previous line of stitching.
Press. You should see three rows of stitching on the inside.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

tips.title: Narrow shirt hem with fusible web
tips.source: Sandra Miller (Cutting Line Designs), Threads magazine
tips.steps:
Overlock the raw hem edge.
Turn the overlocked edge to the wrong side and press, holding the narrow fold with pins. Trim bulk from the folded area.
Turn up a second time and press.
Hold the fold in place with paper-backed fusible web tape.
Edgestitch the narrow hem.
Check the front hem doesn't stick out past the front placket.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

tips.title: Coverstitch hem on knits
tips.steps:
Thread the cover hem needles (usually the outer two). Check your manual for which positions.
If your machine has a knife, lower or disengage it.
Sew a test on a scrap of the same fabric. If stitches bunch, lengthen the stitch; if the fabric stretches or puckers, adjust the differential feed.
For tunnelling (a ridge between the needle rows), adjust the differential feed, lightly starch or stabilise lightweight fabric, and loosen needle tension slightly.
Press the hem up, line it up with the foot's guide markings, start just before or after a seam, and keep the fabric moving steadily.
To finish, turn the handwheel to raise the needles, lift the foot and pull the fabric gently straight back so the threads release from the looper.
Turn the garment inside out, pull the looper thread to the back and tie it off or weave it into the seam.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements. Applies to the Janome CoverPro 1000CPX; check its manual for needle positions.

tips.title: Flat, smooth elastic waistbands
tips.steps:
Remove the seam allowance at the marked waistline. Cut elastic snug but comfortable around your waist, ends butted together. Finish every edge except the waist.
Medium and heavy fabrics: add a 5 cm (2") deep casing above the waistline to garment and lining. Join with a 6 mm (1/4") seam, press toward the lining, fold the casing to the inside, pin and stitch in the ditch, leaving 7.5 cm (3") open at centre back. Use 2 cm (3/4") non-roll elastic.
Sheers or reversible skirts: add a 2 cm (3/4") casing to the underskirt only, join with a narrow zigzag at 1 cm (3/8"), wrap the underskirt over the seam and leave 7.5 cm open. Thread 6 mm (1/4") elastic through and stitch close to its lower edge with a zipper foot so it can't twist.
Partial-stretch band for a tailored front: make a 5.7 cm (2 1/4") deep band with 2 cm non-roll elastic, attach, fold over and stitch in the ditch with an opening at centre back.
Thread the elastic in, stitch across the band at each end of the flat front section, join the elastic ends, spread the gathers and close the opening.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements. A reader comment questions the band-length wording in the original (add dart and pleat depth rather than subtract); test on a toile first.

tips.title: Free-hanging trouser waistband facing
tips.steps:
Cut the inner waistband slightly deeper than the outer so it fully covers the waist seam allowances.
Leave the lower edge of the inner band (or facing) unstitched so it hangs free.
Sew the outer waistband to the trousers.
Press the waist seam open for a flat finish.
Overlock the hidden raw edges so they don't fray.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements. Part of the original is for paying Threads members only, so these steps cover only the free part.

tips.title: Narrow 6 mm mitred corner
tips.steps:
Fold the corner to the wrong side so each edge of the folded triangle is 2 cm (3/4") long, and press.
Trim the pressed triangle, leaving 6 mm (1/4") beyond the fold.
Turn each side edge in 6 mm and press.
Turn each side in another 6 mm and press again. The corner forms a neat mitre.
Stitch the folded edge.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

tips.title: Sharp collar points: stitch across the corner
tips.steps:
Sew upper collar and undercollar right sides together, pivoting at each corner.
Instead of a sharp pivot, take a short diagonal across the point: 1 stitch for lightweight shirting or linen, up to 3 for wool coating.
Trim the seam allowances.
Turn right side out and press. Bulkier fabrics will give slightly softer points.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

tips.title: French seam
tips.steps:
Sew wrong sides together at 1 cm (3/8").
Trim to 3-6 mm (1/8-1/4").
Press the allowances to one side, then fold right sides together with the seam on the fold.
Stitch 6 mm (1/4") from the fold, enclosing the raw edges. An overlocker can do the first pass.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

tips.title: Flat-felled seam
tips.steps:
Sew the seam and press the allowances open.
Trim one allowance to 3 mm (1/8").
Fold the wider allowance over the trimmed one, along a staystitched line, and press.
Edgestitch close to the fold, then edgestitch again near the seam.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

tips.title: Hong Kong seam finish
tips.steps:
Cut narrow bias strips from lining or silk.
Sew a strip to each open seam allowance, right sides together.
Fold the strip away from the seam and press.
Wrap the strip around the raw edge to the back and stitch in the ditch to hold it.
Trim the excess strip and press the allowances open.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

tips.title: Understitching a facing
tips.steps:
Trim both seam allowances to about 6 mm (1/4") and clip every 12 mm (1/2") or so, just short of the seamline. Stagger the clips on the two layers. Don't press yet.
Place the facing right side up under the foot, garment to the left, allowances underneath the facing.
Straight stitch on the facing 3 mm (1/8") from the seamline, through facing and allowances.
Don't stretch or flatten the curve; let the clipped allowances spread.
Press. The facing should roll to the inside and stay there.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

tips.title: Staystitching curves and bias edges
tips.steps:
Staystitch straight after cutting, before handling: necklines, armholes, V-necks, square necks, placket openings and unset godets.
Sew in the direction of the grain, usually from the shoulder down toward the centre.
Stitch 1.5-3 mm (1/16-1/8") inside the seamline, in the seam allowance, with a normal 2 mm stitch. Never cross the seamline.
Don't stretch or straighten the curve as you sew.
Inside corners: stop about 2.5 cm short of the point and restart 2.5 cm past it. V-necks: stitch around in one pass, pivoting at the point.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements. Part of the original is for paying Threads members only, so these steps cover only the free part.

tips.title: Binding a knit jewel neckline (set-up)
tips.steps:
Construct the garment and finish the neckline last.
Cut binding 3.8 cm (1 1/2") wide for lightweight or striped knits, about 5 cm (2") for heavy knits, on the crossgrain or bias.
Cut it 5 cm longer than the neckline measurement.
Mark centre front and centre back on the neckline.
Start at centre back, fold under the binding end and pin.
Stretch the binding lightly and pin every 2-2.5 cm around the neck, back to the start.
Overlap at the start and trim the excess.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements. Part of the original is for paying Threads members only, so these steps cover only the free part. The stitching steps are in the members-only part.

tips.title: Binding over bulky seam intersections
tips.steps:
Trim a small wedge out of the shoulder seam allowance where the binding will cover it, without cutting the seam stitching.
As the foot reaches the bulky seam, stop, lift the foot and let the seam flatten.
Lengthen the stitch slightly and guide the fabric by hand across the bump so the stitching stays straight.
Once past it, return to your normal stitch length.
A foot with a height-release button helps; the same trick works for coverstitched hems and overlocking thick crossings.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

tips.title: Invisible zip into a seam with a facing
tips.source: Kirsten Schaefer, The Assembly Line Sewing Journal
tips.steps:
Press along the seamline to make a crease that guides your stitching.
Lay the zip face down on the right side, teeth on the crease, top stop sitting one seam allowance below the top edge.
Optional: baste down the centre of the tape about 5 mm from its edge with a long stitch.
With an invisible zip foot (or regular zip foot), uncurl the teeth with your fingers and stitch right beside them, down to the notch.
Close the zip, mark where cross seams meet, and sew the other side to match, mirroring the first.
Below the zip, sew the rest of the seam with a regular zip foot, starting just above the end of the zip stitching and about 2-3 mm to the side. Hold the tape out of the way.
Sew the facing on, trimming zip tape above the stop to reduce bulk, turn, and edgestitch the facing about 3 mm from the seam, starting 4-5 cm from the zip. Press.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements. Written for The Assembly Line Tulip Dress (5 mm seam allowance); use your pattern's allowance.

tips.title: Better machine buttonholes
tips.steps:
Always test first on the same fabric, interfacing, layers and grain, and check each test fits the button.
Narrow the bead for fine fabrics, widen it for bulky ones; a slightly longer stitch looks more like ready-to-wear and is more flexible.
Use cotton thread for most wovens, polyester for knits and stretch wovens.
Next to a seam or edge, level the foot with a height-compensating plate or folded paper. Add tear-away or paper underneath to stop tunnelling.
Only use seam sealant if the fabric frays badly, and test it first.
Cut open with pins across each bar tack as stops, or with a buttonhole chisel on a wooden block.
To remove a bad buttonhole, work from the wrong side with a fine seam ripper, a few stitches at a time.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

tips.title: Identical patch pockets with water-soluble thread
tips.source: Reader tip from Jean Morgan, Threads magazine
tips.steps:
Cut the two pocket pieces and place them right sides together.
Wind water-soluble thread on the bobbin; normal thread in the needle.
Sew around three sides, leaving the top open.
Turn right side out and press the seam crisply on the edge with a dry iron.
Steam well. The bobbin thread dissolves and you have two matching pockets with pressed edges.
Finish the top edges and attach.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

tips.title: Reduce bulk on in-seam pockets
tips.steps:
Alter the pattern so the back pocket bag is cut in one with the back piece at the side seam, removing a seam.
Drop the separate front pocket bag.
Staystitch and interface the pocket opening edges, and clip the allowances so the pocket can fold into place.
Sew the side seams.
Fold the back pocket bag forward to the front.
Topstitch the bag to the inside of the front so it lies flat with no ridge at the side seam.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements. Part of the original is for paying Threads members only, so these steps cover only the free part.

tips.title: Cheater's ease for sleeve caps
tips.steps:
Best on crisp fabrics such as cotton shirting.
Before setting the sleeve in, work on the sleeve cap seam allowance.
Push and crimp the seam allowance with your fingers to build shape into the cap. No ease stitching needed.
Check the crimped cap against the armhole and adjust until it matches.
Pin and set the sleeve in.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements. A reader alternative: run the fabric under the foot with your finger pressed behind it (ease-plussing).

tips.title: Attaching a shirt cuff
tips.source: Sandra Miller (Cutting Line Designs), Threads magazine
tips.steps:
Check the cuff markings first.
Sew the non-interfaced cuff layer to the sleeve.
Sew the interfaced layer to it, following the markings.
Press the seam flat before trimming, then trim and grade, notching curves, and press open on a point presser.
Turn the cuff right side out, roll the seam slightly to the inside and press.
Turn under the 1.5 cm (5/8") allowance on the open edge, press and grade.
Edgestitch the cuff from the right side, starting at its centre.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements. Part of the original is for paying Threads members only, so these steps cover only the free part.

tips.title: Flat dart points without tying off
tips.steps:
Sew from the wide end at 2.5 mm, shortening to 1.5 mm for the last 6 mm (1/4") before the point.
Method 1: sew right off the fold at the point and keep going about 2 cm (3/4") into air, then cut the chain. Test first; some machines dislike this.
Method 2: stop at the point, needle down at the fold, lift the foot, pull the fabric back about 2.5 cm, reposition and stitch 6 mm into the dart allowance to lock it.
Method 3 (fine tight weaves like shirting): at a thread's width from the fold drop to 1.0 mm and take four stitches along the fold, then secure into the allowance.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

tips.title: Even gathers every time
tips.steps:
Divide the gathered edge and the flat edge into the same number of equal sections and mark them.
Sew three or four parallel rows of long straight stitch about 3 mm (1/8") apart (about 3 mm stitch for light to medium fabric). Don't backstitch; leave long tails.
Pull the bobbin threads from one end only, gathering to a bit under half the flat length. Pulling top and bobbin together locks the stitches.
Repeat from the other end and wind the threads around a pin in a figure eight.
Pin the flat piece taut on a padded surface, match the marks, and spread the gathers evenly with an awl.
Sew between two gathering rows with the gathered side up, then pull out the visible gathering thread and press the gathers in the seam allowance.
Typical fullness is 2 to 2.5 times the finished length. Stay a bias flat edge first.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

tips.title: Continuous sleeve placket
tips.steps:
Mark the pleats and the top of the slit (usually about 10 cm or a little more). Do both sleeves together.
Cut two strips about 22 cm (8 3/4") long and 3.8-5 cm (1 1/2-2") wide.
Press a 6-10 mm (1/4-3/8") fold along one long edge.
Pin the strip right side to the wrong side of the opening, raw edges together, spreading the slit straight. A slight dip at the centre is normal.
Sew at 6-10 mm, going just past the V while keeping the strip's allowance even.
Fold the pressed edge over the seamline and edgestitch it down.
Press flat and stitch a diagonal across the top of the placket on the inside.
Form the pleats, pin and press lightly.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements. Part of the original is for paying Threads members only, so these steps cover only the free part.

tips.title: Bagging a jacket lining by machine
tips.steps:
Overlock the allowances on jacket and lining. Add a back neck facing to the lining pattern if needed.
Sew jacket and lining, leaving an opening in one lining side seam. Baste the jacket hem up 6 mm and press lightly.
Sew the lining to the front facings, leaving the bottom 7.5 cm (3") of the facings open.
Check lining and jacket widths match at hem, sides and sleeves.
Sew lining to jacket around the fronts and neck in one seam, then sew the hems right sides together, matching side seams.
Turn right side out through the side-seam opening.
Machine-stitch the sleeve lining hems to the sleeve hems.
Close the lining opening with a ladder stitch.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements. Part of the original is for paying Threads members only, so these steps cover only the free part.

tips.title: Fusing interfacing where it counts
tips.steps:
Fuse to the outer cuff and upper collar, not the facing or undercollar, so seam allowances don't shadow through.
Patch pockets: interface the top with a strip aligned to the fold line.
Interfacing both collar layers? Use a lighter weight.
Knit hems: overlock a crossgrain strip of fusible to the hem edge, fuse with steam, then hand catchstitch loosely.
Stretch fabrics: cut knit interfacing so its stretch runs the same way as the fabric's.
Softer jacket fronts: fuse to a cotton batiste underlining instead of the fashion fabric.
Use a silk organza press cloth so you can see what you're doing.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements. Part of the original is for paying Threads members only, so these steps cover only the free part. Heat and time settings are in the members-only part; follow the interfacing maker's instructions.

tips.title: Stable topstitched hems on soft knits
tips.steps:
Press the hem up using a card template so it's even.
Before assembly, fuse 12 mm (1/2") strips of bias knit fusible interfacing to the wrong side of the hem allowance.
Soft knits stretch most across the grain, so this stops the hem rippling as you stitch.
After construction, fuse the hem in place.
Topstitch from the right side with two rows of straight stitching. The author prefers this to a twin needle, which can tunnel and ripple.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

tips.title: Pressing tips from an alterations pro
tips.steps:
Press every seam as you go; nobody can reach inside seams properly once a garment's finished.
Test steam and pressure on scraps; it's easy to overpress, especially synthetics.
Have a ham, sleeve board, seam roll, clapper and point presser to hand.
Slide paper strips under seam allowances and darts so they don't imprint on the right side.
Hold a crease with the blunt end of a point turner while the fabric cools.
To remove bagging at knees or seat: flatten, steam, pat smooth, then press firmly.
Use a press cloth or a non-stick iron shoe so you can press firmly without shine or scorching.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

tips.title: Laying out and cutting accurately
tips.steps:
Take your time; small cutting errors add up and distort the garment.
Napped, pile and one-way prints need every piece facing the same direction.
Straighten the cross edge, then line up each grainline with the lengthwise grain.
Lay brown paper under the fabric and pin through it, like production cutters, to stop slippery fabric shifting.
Stripes and plaids: match the layers and transfer stripe marks across connecting pieces.
Use pattern weights rather than lots of pins; keep any pins inside the cutting line.
Cut with long smooth strokes using sharp shears.
tips.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements. Part of the original is for paying Threads members only, so these steps cover only the free part.

tips.title: Which embroidery stabiliser for which fabric
tips.steps:
Knits and sweatshirts: cut-away. Light Cut-away for light knits or low stitch counts; one layer of Medium Cut-away for medium to heavy knits such as sweatshirts and polos.
Wovens: tear-away. Soft-away suits most wovens; Fusible Soft-away for slippery wovens like satin and poplin.
Towelling and napped fabrics: hoop wash-away underneath and lay a water-soluble topper (Supersolv) on top so the pile doesn't swallow the stitches.
Sheers and lace: wash-away. Soft semi-sheer fabrics: See-through Cut-away.
Hoop the stabiliser with the garment where you can; for awkward items, hoop the stabiliser and baste the garment to it.
After stitching, trim cut-away to about 6 mm around the design.
For scratchy designs (metallic thread, or anything for children) iron a soft cover-up interfacing over the back.
tips.notes: [Web source] Summarised by Claude from Echidna Sewing's stabiliser guide. Product names are Echidna's range; for the Brother NV880E.

tips.title: Folded-top elastic waistband
tips.notes: [From your Facebook saved reels] Steps written from the reel's caption, not the video. Check against the video.
tips.steps:
After sewing crotch and side seams, overlock the waist edge.
Cut elastic to your length, overlap the ends and stitch securely.
Mark the elastic in quarters to match centre front, centre back and side seams.
Pin the elastic to the inside top edge, matching the marks.
Sew the top edge of the elastic to the waist edge, stretching the elastic as you sew.
Turn it to the inside to encase the elastic and pin.
Topstitch along the lower edge of the elastic, stretching as you sew.

tips.title: Sewing a T-shirt like a pro in 7 steps
tips.source: The Last Stitch (Fit for Knits) (Facebook reel)
tips.notes: [From your Facebook saved reels] Steps written from the reel's caption, not the video. Check against the video.
tips.steps:
Sewing order: shoulders, neckband, sleeves, side seams, hem.
Stabilise shoulder seams with clear elastic or a light stable tape so they don't grow.
Place the neckband seam slightly away from the shoulder seam; it hides the join and reduces bulk.
Sew sleeves in flat, right sides together, matching notches.
Sew side and sleeve seams in one pass, from the hem to the sleeve end.
Press seam allowances in opposite directions before hemming to flatten the layers.
Start hemming on the back, slightly away from a side seam, so the overlap is hidden and stitches don't skip.

tips.steps:
A sleeve cap slightly longer than the armhole is normal; that's sleeve ease and it lets you move.

tips.title: Reversible or fully lined sleeveless dress, all seams hidden
tips.notes: [From your Instagram saved posts] Steps written from the post's caption, not the video. Check against the post.
tips.steps:
Cut front and back in both fabrics (call them A and B). Skip facings. Sew any darts.
Pin A and B fronts right sides together at neckline and armholes; sew at the pattern seam allowance.
Clip seam allowances where needed, turn right side out, press so neither fabric shows on the other side, and topstitch.
Repeat for the two backs.
Put the back inside the front, matching A to A and B to B, and sew the shoulder seams. Pull through and press.
Lay flat with A right sides together and B right sides together, and sew each side seam in one continuous line from the A hem, through the underarm, to the B hem. Turn right side out.

fitting.title: Full bust adjustment (darted bodice)
fitting.symptom: Tight across the bust, strain lines pointing to the bust, front riding up. If cut to full bust instead, too loose at shoulders and upper chest.
fitting.cause: Your cup size is bigger than the one the pattern was drafted for. Measure full bust minus high bust: every 2.5 cm is one cup (A 2.5, B 5, C 7.5, D 10 cm). Subtract the pattern's cup, then halve it; that's how far you spread the pattern.
fitting.fix:
Trace the front bodice.
Mark your bust point on it (hold it against you).
Draw lines: through the dart to the bust point, from the waist (or hem) up to the bust point, from the bust point up to the armhole, and a horizontal line low on the piece.
Cut along them, stopping just short of the bust point and armhole seamline so the pieces stay hinged.
On paper, spread the side section out by your halved amount, keeping the cut edges parallel. The dart opens wider.
Drop the lower centre section so the hem lines up again.
Redraw the dart legs to the bust point, take in the lower side seam if needed, and true the armhole, hem and centre front.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Swayback: pooling above the seat
fitting.symptom: Horizontal folds across the lower back just above the seat, mainly at centre back. Side seams still hang straight.
fitting.cause: Centre back is longer than your back between waist and seat, often with a deeper lumbar curve.
fitting.fix:
On a toile, pin out the fold at centre back until it's smooth. The depth is usually 1-3 cm and tapers to nothing at the side seams.
On the back pattern, draw a horizontal line at the wrinkle height from centre back almost to the side seam.
Cut from centre back, leaving a hinge at the side seam.
Overlap at centre back by the pinned amount, pivoting on the side seam so its length doesn't change.
Redraw centre back as a smooth line and true the waist and darts.
With a waist seam, take it out of the back bodice and skirt at the waist instead.
Trousers (Tilly and the Buttons): measure down the centre back seam by the amount, draw a smooth line to the top of the side seam, and re-shape any darts.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Broad back: tight across the back
fitting.symptom: Back feels tight while the front fits; fabric strains at the back armholes and they pull toward the centre back.
fitting.cause: Your back is wider than the pattern's back.
fitting.fix:
Measure: slash the toile vertically each side of the back and see how far it needs to spread, or add 1.2-2.5 cm and re-test.
On the back piece, draw a line down from the shoulder, then turn at right angles to the side seam below the armhole.
Draw a short line from that vertical line out to the armhole where you need the most width.
Cut down the vertical and across to the side seam allowance, leaving a hinge; cut the short line to the armhole allowance, leaving a second hinge.
Swing the side section out until the gap is half the total width you need.
Keep the shoulder hinged, trace, and smooth shoulder and armhole. The armhole length doesn't change, so the sleeve doesn't need altering.
Over about 2 cm, use the original's alternative method with a back shoulder dart.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Forward shoulder
fitting.symptom: Shoulder seam sits behind the top of your shoulder, the garment slides back, the front neckline rides up and the back neck may gape.
fitting.cause: Shoulders roll slightly forward. Desk work and long sessions hunched over a machine add to it.
fitting.fix:
On a toile, mark where the shoulder seam should sit and measure how far it needs to move (all along, or just at the shoulder end).
On the front, draw a new shoulder seamline lower by that amount and trim the extra.
On the back, add paper and raise the shoulder seamline by the same amount.
Check front and back shoulder seams still match in length.
For sleeves, rotate the sleeve forward to match: move the cap notch forward so it meets the new shoulder seam.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Sloping or square shoulders
fitting.symptom: Flat (square) shoulders: the neck end of the shoulder seam points up toward your ears. Sloping shoulders: strain at the neck end of the shoulder seam.
fitting.cause: Your shoulder angle differs from the pattern's.
fitting.fix:
Measure on a toile: pinch out excess at the shoulder (sloping) or slash and spread (square).
Remove the seam allowance from front and back.
Flat shoulders: mark the pinched amount down from the neck end of the shoulder seam. Sloping shoulders: add paper and extend the neck end up by your amount.
Rule a new shoulder line from that mark to the original armhole end.
Cut the new line, add seam allowance back, and do the same on the back.
The armhole is unchanged, so the sleeve doesn't need altering.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements. Seamwork calls square shoulders 'flat'. Its method changes the neck end of the shoulder seam only.

fitting.title: Gaping neckline
fitting.symptom: Neckline stands away from your chest; you can see down the front, worse when leaning forward.
fitting.cause: More fabric at the neckline than your upper chest needs. First check the neckline hasn't stretched in sewing (staystitch bias necklines).
fitting.fix:
On the toile, pin the excess into a small dart each side of the neckline until it lies flat; measure the dart width.
On the front, draw a line from the bust dart to the apex, and from the apex up to the neckline where you pinned.
Draw the neckline dart to the apex and cut it out.
Cut the bust dart line to just short of the apex.
Swing the upper section to close the neckline dart; the bust dart opens wider.
Tape, trace, smooth the neckline and redraw the bust dart with equal legs.
Dartless pattern, gape up to 12 mm: fold the dart out of the pattern and smooth the neckline.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.
fitting.garmentFix: Reader suggestion in the comments (not the author's): stitch small tucks or darts radiating from the neckline, inside or as a feature.

fitting.title: Gaping over the upper chest: check the cause first
fitting.symptom: Neckline or upper chest gapes, often with a hollow chest or narrow shoulders.
fitting.cause: Possible causes: neckline stretched to fit the lining (ease the bigger edge into the smaller one instead); stiff or heavy interfacing or lining; straps set too wide; size chosen by full bust rather than upper bust.
fitting.fix:
Rule out the causes above first.
Sew a toile to confirm the adjustment is needed and how much to remove.
Remove a small amount along the neckline only, keeping the change small.
The step-by-step is in the linked video, not the article.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Armhole too low or too high
fitting.symptom: Too low: underarm seam sits well below the armpit, extra fabric over the upper chest, can't lift your arms. Too high: tight and uncomfortable at the underarm, strain across the upper chest.
fitting.cause: Armhole depth doesn't match your body.
fitting.fix:
Measure on a toile: pinch out the excess (too low) or work out the length to add (too high).
Remove seam allowances.
Draw horizontal lines above the notches on front, back and sleeve cap, and cut along them.
Too low: overlap the pieces by your amount. Too high: spread them by your amount over paper.
Tape, smooth the edges, extend grainlines if you lengthened, and add seam allowance back. The sleeve cap changes with the armhole.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Full bicep
fitting.symptom: Sleeves regularly tight on the upper arm, no room to layer.
fitting.cause: Your upper arm plus ease is bigger than the sleeve. Adjustment = your bicep minus the sleeve width (without seam allowances) plus the ease you want (knits little or none; fitted wovens 2.5-7.5 cm).
fitting.fix:
Trace the sleeve.
Draw a line from the top of the cap to the hem, parallel to the grain, and a line across at the widest point.
Cut both lines to just short of the seam allowance, leaving hinges.
Spread the sides out until the gap equals your adjustment, and tape paper behind.
Up to 2.5 cm: smooth the cap and straighten the hem.
Over 2.5 cm: retrace the original cap curve and add half the extra to the bodice by lowering the armhole or widening the side seam.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Waist too big or too small
fitting.symptom: Too big: fabric stands away at the back or sides, bunches, slides around. Too small: constricting, worse sitting down.
fitting.cause: Waist measurement falls in a different size from bust or hips.
fitting.fix:
Sew a toile with basted seams and pin where the waist gapes or pulls.
Too big: deepen the darts or add new ones, or take in the side seams.
Too small: let out the side seams if there's room, or add narrow side panels.
Redraw the waistline with a curved ruler so the change blends.
Make the same change to facings, waistbands and linings, and update the paper pattern.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Gaping back waist on jeans
fitting.symptom: Jeans fit the hips but gape at the centre back waist.
fitting.cause: Waist smaller in proportion to hips than the jeans were cut for.
fitting.fix: Not a pattern fix; see the finished-garment fix.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.
fitting.garmentFix:
Pinch out the excess at centre back waist and pin.
Chalk both sides of the pinned section and measure it.
Up to 2.5-3.8 cm: one centre-back dart. More than 5 cm: two darts, about 6-9 cm either side of centre back.
Split the excess between the darts, drawing them from the waistband down to stop 2.5-5 cm above the fullest part of the seat.
Stitch, tapering to the point; sew off the edge and knot rather than backstitching.
Press, trim and overlock the edges.

fitting.title: Full tummy (trousers)
fitting.source: Nikki Hoar, Tilly and the Buttons
fitting.symptom: Drag lines across the stomach, tight front crotch, side seams pulled forward.
fitting.cause: Front needs more room over the tummy while the rest fits.
fitting.fix:
Extend the grainline to the waist on the front leg.
Draw a horizontal line from crotch to side seam at your fullest point.
Draw a vertical line from the waist down to meet it, and a diagonal from that meeting point to the top of the side seam.
Cut the horizontal from the crotch to the vertical, cut the diagonal, and cut down the vertical from the waist, leaving hinges.
Spread the top to add width and length. Start with 15 mm; that's 30 mm across the whole front.
Redraw the crotch curve, waistline and grainline smoothly.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Full hips on a straight skirt
fitting.symptom: Drag lines across the skirt, skewed grain, looks too small rather than sleek, extra fullness at the high hip looks wrong.
fitting.cause: Small waist relative to full hips.
fitting.fix:
Measure hips at 7.5, 15 and 23 cm (3, 6, 9") below the waist, front and back separately, and check ease sitting down.
Start from a pattern that fits your waist.
Slide the side sections out to add hip width, pivoting at the waist.
Aim for 5-6.5 cm (2-2 1/2") total ease at the fullest hip; front and back can differ.
Lay front over back to check side seams match, and pin-fit sitting down before sewing.
Waist: sew darts at right angles to the edge in the seam allowance, allow about 2.5 cm ease into the band, and run three rows of 2 mm stitching on the waist seamline to ease it in.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Full seat (trousers)
fitting.symptom: Diagonal creases across the bum running toward the back crotch seam; waistband dips at the back.
fitting.cause: Back crotch seam too short for your seat.
fitting.fix:
Remove side seam allowance on the back leg.
Draw a diagonal from the middle of the back crotch seam to the side seam.
Cut from the crotch seam almost to the side seam, leaving a hinge.
Pivot the top section up and away by 10-15 mm and tape over paper.
Redraw the crotch seam straight and add seam allowance back.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Flat seat (trousers)
fitting.symptom: Loose fabric under the bum and diagonal wrinkles running up toward the hip.
fitting.cause: Back crotch seam longer than your seat needs.
fitting.fix:
Remove side seam allowance on the back leg.
Draw a diagonal from the middle of the back crotch seam to the side seam.
Cut from the crotch seam almost to the side seam, leaving a hinge.
Pivot the top section down to overlap, starting at about 15 mm, and tape.
Redraw the crotch seam straight and add seam allowance back.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Rise too long or too short
fitting.symptom: Too long: extra fabric you can pinch out horizontally on a toile. Too short: tall sewists, waist sitting lower than intended.
fitting.cause: Your torso length from crotch to waist differs from the pattern's.
fitting.fix:
Measure your rise with a flexible tape and compare to the pattern without seam allowances.
Shorter torso: pinch out the excess on a toile to find the amount.
Draw lengthen or shorten lines at right angles to the grain and change front, back and any side panels by the same amount.
Keep the grainline aligned.
Check zip, fly, pocket and facing pieces also need changing, then sew another toile.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Front crotch too long or too short
fitting.source: Nikki Hoar, Tilly and the Buttons
fitting.symptom: Too long: drag lines down from the front crotch. Too short: lines up from the front crotch, feels short there. Horizontal folds across the front crotch: flat pelvis. Vertical lines: rounder pelvis.
fitting.cause: Front crotch extension or curve doesn't suit your shape.
fitting.fix:
Too long: mark 10 mm in from the end of the front crotch seam and redraw the inseam to taper into it. Trim a little at a time.
Too short: add paper and extend the crotch point by 10-15 mm, tapering the inseam back to the original.
Flat pelvis: make the front crotch curve slightly shallower.
Rounder pelvis: make it slightly deeper and let out the side seams a little.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Full thigh
fitting.symptom: Tight across the upper thigh; diagonal wrinkles across the back leg toward the crotch.
fitting.cause: Not enough room at the top of the leg.
fitting.fix:
On the back leg, extend the crotch point about 6 mm (1/4") and curve back into the inseam.
Do the same on the front leg.
Sew a new toile.
Still tight? Add another 6 mm and re-test, in small steps.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Full calf
fitting.symptom: Tight around the calves; fabric bunching behind the knees.
fitting.cause: Calf plus ease bigger than the pattern's lower leg.
fitting.fix:
Measure your calf against the pattern at the same height, or slash a toile and see how far it spreads.
On the back leg, mark A at the fullest calf height, centre of the leg, and B 5 cm above it.
Draw a line from B to the hem, and diagonals from B to the side seam and to the inseam about 5 cm below the crotch.
Cut up the centre line and along both diagonals to the seam allowance, hinged at B.
Spread until the gap at A equals the width you need.
Trace, then either keep the width to the hem or taper back in at the hem.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Excess fabric under the bum or back thigh
fitting.source: Nikki Hoar, Tilly and the Buttons
fitting.symptom: Spare fabric across the back of the upper thigh or under the seat.
fitting.cause: Back leg too long for your thigh at that height.
fitting.fix:
Pin out the extra fabric across the back thigh on your toile and mark where it sits on the pattern.
Draw a line across the back leg between those points, and a second line from a third of the way along up to the crotch seam.
Cut along the second line, then the first, stopping 15 mm from the side seams.
Overlap the upper section by the pinned amount and tape.
Redraw the leg seams and crotch seam smoothly.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Lengthening or shortening a bodice
fitting.symptom: Waist seam sits above or below your natural waist; hem in the wrong place.
fitting.cause: Your vertical measurements differ from the pattern's.
fitting.fix:
Measure the bodice front, back and skirt without seam allowances and compare to your own lengths (including centre back length if listed).
Use the lengthen/shorten line, or draw one below the bust shaping.
Draw a vertical guide line across it at right angles.
Lengthen: cut, spread by your amount over paper keeping the guide line straight, tape and smooth the sides.
Shorten: draw a second line your amount away, fold or cut out the strip, overlap using the guide line, tape and smooth.
Large changes: split them across more than one line.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements.

fitting.title: Blending between sizes
fitting.symptom: Bust, waist and hips fall into different sizes.
fitting.cause: Pattern sizes assume set proportions between measurements.
fitting.fix:
Trace both sizes you need.
Lay a hip curve between the larger size's line and the smaller size's line at the adjustment point.
Adjust until the transition looks smooth, then draw it.
Do the same on matching seams so front and back still sew together; check seam lengths match.
Go over the final cutting line in a darker colour.
fitting.notes: [Web source] Steps summarised by Claude from the linked article, with inches converted to metric. Check the original before relying on measurements. The tip about checking matching seam lengths is Claude's addition, not from the article.
